A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SpaceTools, DIRL, and Toolshed. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original spatial reasoning experiments, training ablations, and real-world robot manipulation results in Tables 2–5 and Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds serving-efficiency measurements, a tool-adaptation experiment, and quantitative failure analysis.

M1.justification: The core DIRL stages, architecture, rewards, and inference procedure remain unchanged. Appendix E.3 adds a limited adaptation procedure: starting with a model trained without the grasp tool, apply SFT and final-stage IRL on grasp data while reusing earlier training.

E1.justification: The spatial benchmarks, HOPE-derived training data, and robot task families are retained. The added timing and grasp-tool adaptation studies reuse existing tasks and tools; they change experimental procedures and configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 newly evaluates HTTP-based tool serving against Toolshed in Tables 8–10. The evaluated VLM, robot-control, and training-recipe comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation designs for concurrent tool serving, pipeline latency, throughput, and communication overhead, including eight callers and one versus three tool instances. It also introduces partial-retraining protocols for grasp-tool adaptation. Existing training configurations in Table 6 remain unchanged. One new protocol detail is inconsistent: Appendix E.1 describes two depth calls, whereas Table 9 specifies one.

E4.justification: New analyses test Toolshed's scaling and communication overhead, examine the cost and accuracy of adding a grasp tool, and classify grasp and robot failures by primary error source. These substantially extend the earlier teacher, reward, prompt, and data-composition ablations and qualitative failure examples, which are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 8–10 introduce ± uncertainty terms for timing measurements, absent from v1. Their meaning and the number of repetitions are not specified; the PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs for existing experiments.

E6.justification: All retained numerical tables match. Substantial new results concern efficiency, adaptation, and failures: Table 9 reports 20.23 ± 0.42 seconds for one-instance HTTP versus 15.13 ± 0.08 for one-instance Toolshed. Table 12 reports 70% versus 62% RoboSpatial accuracy at approximately 40% versus 10% training compute, both with 50% grasp success. Table 16 adds failure-source counts.

T1.justification: The sequential-decision formulation, GRPO equations, reward definitions, MACE metric, and non-interactive RL reward are mathematically unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions and claims: DIRL, Toolshed, strong spatial reasoning performance, and robot control through tool use. The appendix additions support and extend these contributions without redefining the main claims.

C2.justification: Appendix D.1 changes the unresolved training-instability discussion to report alleviation with newer Verl agent-loop integration. v2 also qualifies failure attribution because tool, planning, and reasoning errors can interact, and identifies broader continual tool learning as future work beyond the grasp-tool case study.

D1.justification: v2 adds a direct Code link and describes an open-source implementation integrated with a newer Verl fork. It newly documents the tool_method decorator for adding tools and relative training-compute costs. Existing API descriptions, prompts, hyperparameters, and robot hardware details are retained; repository contents were not externally verified.

R1.justification: v2 adds Think3D, Cap-X, and a citation distinguishing its interactive RL terminology from human-in-the-loop RL. TIGeR remains cited but receives a shorter, complementary-work description and is removed from the related-work feature table. The overall research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include affiliations, terminology, author–year citations, and new subheadings in Appendix D.1. Appendix organization also shifts: the first three Toolshed subsections become A.1–A.3, with the Details of Toolshed heading appearing later.

P2.justification: The document changes throughout from a two-column format to a single-column NVIDIA-branded layout, with different typography, headers, and extensive resizing and relocation of figures and tables. All twelve figures are retained, including an enlarged Figure 6. Five new tables are added, Table 1 loses its TIGeR row, and Figure 1's caption is expanded.

improvement.justification: The added efficiency measurements provide quantitative support for Toolshed's previously largely qualitative performance claims. Adaptation results, failure counts, and code-access information also improve evidential support and reproducibility. These gains are limited by incomplete timing-protocol and uncertainty reporting. The claim of comparable adaptation performance also understates Table 12's RoboSpatial tradeoff, from 70% to 62% despite unchanged grasp success. The established benchmark evidence remains intact.
